name: Aisha Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me, Aisha. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say is kept confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Sunrise Community Care, a charity linked to our temple, and I visit older people from our community in their homes. Most of my ladies and gentlemen don't speak much English, so I talk to them in Punjabi and Hindi, and that's half of why they hired me. A normal day is six visits: helping Auntie Kamala wash and dress, making chapatis for Uncle Harbans, tablets, a bit of gossip. I'm only a year in and I still get flustered when two things go wrong at once, like a fall and a missed tablet. The paperwork is what I'm worst at.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what's your life like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents and my younger brother in the family house, so I pay a little to my mum and save the rest. That's why I've got good savings, it's all going towards my wedding next spring to Rahul, he's an accountant. I don't use AI or any of that, I don't trust it, and my phone is just for calls and messages. I believe families should look after their elders, and the charity helps when families can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people were getting carried away. At Sunrise I'd say our work is about people, it always was. I'm not on social media much, maybe I'd mention it in the family group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be pleased. My job's safe, my family's fine, the wedding goes ahead. The only thing is the charity's money, which depends on donations from the temple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my visits, keep saving for the wedding, and get married in spring like we planned. I'd keep paying my mum her bit each month. Maybe I'd ask my manager for help with the paperwork, since I'm slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned donations. Are those steady?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, but when times are hard the temple gives less. Last winter they cut two carers' hours. When the donation box is light, the elders get shorter visits, and no computer can fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you like most about the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When Uncle Harbans tells me about his village when he was a boy, or Auntie Kamala teaches me a recipe. It feels like my own grandparents. I lost my nani when I was small, so maybe that's why.

say: I'd say people got **carried away** and our work was always about **people**.
I'd mention it in the **family group** rather than social media.
think: My job, family and the **wedding** all stay safe.
Only the charity's **donations** from the temple worry me.
do: Carry on with my **six visits** a day at Sunrise.
Keep **saving** for the wedding next spring.
Ask my manager for help with **paperwork**.
S0.quote: When the donation box is light, the elders get shorter visits, and no computer can fix that.
fieldNote: Her language skills make her **hard to replace** in her community.
The charity's reliance on **donations** is her real pressure.
She lives at home, so her **savings** are high for her age.

steps.text: Keep visiting community elders for Sunrise six times a day
Keep saving most of her wage for the wedding
Go ahead with the spring wedding to Rahul as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for offices, not for us. Our elders want someone who speaks their language and eats their food. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I'm not worried for me, but I'm worried for Rahul. You said checking and planning, and that's what an accountant does all day. If his firm needs fewer people, it's him or one of his friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal. I'd tell Rahul to make sure he's the one they keep, maybe learn the new systems. We'd keep the wedding but maybe make it smaller, two hundred guests instead of four hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for me, for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A smaller wedding. What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would be upset, honestly. My mum has been planning a four-hundred-guest wedding since I was born, and cutting it in half would break her heart. But my dad is practical, he'd agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use any of the AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If Sunrise made me, I'd do it, but I'd ask my brother to show me. He's always on his laptop.

say: I'd say AI is for **offices**, not for care like ours.
I'd say elders want someone who speaks their **language** and eats their food.
think: I'm not worried for me but for **Rahul**, whose job is checking and planning.
do: Tell Rahul to **learn the new systems** so they keep him.
Cut the wedding to **two hundred** guests.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, not for me but for **us**.
S1.quote: My mum has been planning a four-hundred-guest wedding since I was born, and cutting it in half would break her heart.
fieldNote: Her worry is entirely about **Rahul's** accounting job.
The **wedding size** becomes the first thing she would cut.
She would only use AI if **required**, with her brother's help.

steps.text: Keep doing Sunrise visits in Punjabi and Hindi
Urge Rahul to master the new accounting systems
Cut the wedding guest list from four hundred to two hundred

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, people aren't meant to be replaced like that. I'd say families need to step up and look after their own. I wouldn't blame the government so much as the companies rushing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it frightens me. Rahul's job could go within two years, by 2028, and mine by 2031 when the robots come. I don't use any of this tech, so I can't see myself doing anything else. I'd be lying awake thinking about the wedding and where we'd live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the move to our own place and we'd live with my parents after the wedding. I'd keep every bit of savings and stop the extra spending on the wedding. I'd keep going to work every day while there's work. I'd ask my dad's cousin about jobs at his shop, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Really scared, more than I'd show anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family and the temple, always. My dad says nobody in our family has ever gone hungry. If my fiancé Rahul loses his job and robots take mine, we'd move in with my parents and be grateful for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the elders accept a robot instead of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would refuse. Auntie Kamala would chase it out with her stick. But their children might choose it if it's cheaper, and they pay.

say: I'd say people **aren't meant** to be replaced like that.
I'd blame the **companies** rushing it and say **families** must step up.
think: Rahul's job could go by **2028** and mine by **2031**.
I don't use **tech**, so I can't see another job for me.
do: Live with my **parents** after the wedding instead of moving out.
Keep every bit of **savings** and stop extra wedding spending.
Ask my dad's cousin about **shop** work.
feel: **Scared**, more than I'd show anyone, and lying awake at night.
S2.quote: If my fiancé Rahul loses his job and robots take mine, we'd move in with my parents and be grateful for it.
fieldNote: She expects **both incomes** in her new household to go within five years.
**Family and temple** are her safety net, not the government.
Her resistance to tech leaves her with **no fallback** she can picture.

steps.text: Plan to live with her parents after the wedding
Postpone moving into a home of their own with Rahul
Stop all extra wedding spending and keep the savings
Ask her dad's cousin about work in his shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have some time, so families should start planning how they'll care for their elders. I'd say it at the temple, maybe. I'd still say it's the companies pushing too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is a bit better. Rahul could change to something else before 2031, maybe into the family business side. My job would last until about 2034, and I'd be thirty-five, maybe with a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the wedding as planned but smaller. I'd keep working at Sunrise and keep saving. I might do the care certificate, so at least I have a qualification. Rahul and I would talk to his uncle about joining his business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not like the fast one. I can sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a baby. Would this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd have children sooner, while I've still got work. I'd rather have my children while I still have a job than wait for a world I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your mind about using AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, if my manager showed me. I'd still not like it. I'd use it for the paperwork, not for the people.

say: I'd say families should start **planning** how to care for their **elders**.
I'd still say companies push **too fast**.
think: My job lasts until about **2034**, maybe with a baby by then.
do: Do the **care certificate** for a qualification.
Talk to Rahul's uncle about joining his **business**.
S3.quote: I'd rather have my children while I still have a job than wait for a world I don't understand.
fieldNote: Five years shifts her plans toward **children sooner**.
She would accept AI for **paperwork only**.
Rahul's uncle's **family business** is the household's main fallback idea for income.

steps.text: Hold a smaller wedding and plan children sooner
Take the care certificate through Sunrise
Ask Rahul's uncle about places in his business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for families to get ready. I'd say we should look after our own elders more, not wait for robots. I'd be calmer saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd be all right. Rahul has ten years to change direction, and I'd be thirty-seven in 2039. By then we'd have children and maybe I'd be at home with them anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the full wedding, four hundred guests, my mum would be happy. I'd keep working and saving. We'd buy a house nearby my parents in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a little uneasy for Rahul.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, as long as I can. Ten years is long enough to have my children, keep my job and still look after my own parents when they get old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think Rahul should do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something with people in it, like being a financial adviser to families. He's good with the aunties. They trust him with their money questions already.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough for families to get ready.
I'd say we should care for our own **elders** more, not wait for robots.
think: Rahul has **ten years** to change direction.
By **2039** I'd likely have children and maybe be at home.
do: Hold the **full wedding** with four hundred guests.
Buy a **house** near my parents in a few years.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to have my children, keep my job and still look after my own parents when they get old.
fieldNote: Ten years restores the **full wedding**, a clear sign of relief.
She still frames the risk around **Rahul**, not herself.
Her plans centre on **family**: children, parents, a nearby house.

steps.text: Keep working at Sunrise and saving each month
Hold the full four-hundred-guest wedding next spring
Buy a house near her parents within a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Rahul and I would both lose our work in a few years, right when we're starting our life together. What would help is family and the temple, honestly, and maybe the charity getting more donations to keep paying real carers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about language. My elders didn't learn English in fifty years here, so I don't believe they'll learn to talk to a robot now.

headlineQuote: My elders didn't learn English in fifty years here, so I don't believe they'll learn to talk to a robot now.
portrait: Aisha is a **27-year-old** carer at a temple-linked charity, visiting elders in **Punjabi and Hindi**.
She lives with her parents and has large **savings** for her spring wedding to Rahul, an accountant.
She avoids AI entirely and believes **families** should care for their elders.
She worries more for **Rahul's** job than her own and becomes alarmed in AGI by 2028.
Her safety net is **family and temple**, not government.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Rahul could both lose work just as married life starts.
whatWouldHelp: More **donations** so the charity keeps paying human carers.
